t: #2545 Sort the Students by Their Kth Score
o: We must reorder the rows of a matrix so that the column-k values descend, keeping each row intact. In Example 1, sorting by column 2 (values 9, 11, 3) puts the row with 11 first. Sizes are ≤ 250×250, so a comparison sort is more than enough.
k: Sort whole rows with a comparator on column k.
Scores are distinct, so no tie-breaking is needed.

a.n: Approach 1: Sort rows with a custom comparator
a.i: Most languages let you sort the matrix directly using the k-th entry of each row as the key. Descending order is achieved by comparing b[k] vs a[k] or negating the key.
s: Sort the list of rows using row[k] as key, descending.
a.t: O(m log m · n) — sorting m rows, each comparison reads one column value (rows move by reference)
a.sp: O(m) — or O(log m) depending on the sort implementation; sorting may be in-place

a.i: If you must not mutate the input or your language lacks convenient row comparators, sort the list of row indices by their column-k values and materialize a new matrix in that order.
s: Build the answer by picking rows in index order.
a.t: O(m log m + m·n) — index sort plus rebuilding the matrix

w: Use Approach 1 unless immutability matters. Pitfalls: sorting ascending by mistake, or in JavaScript forgetting that Array.prototype.sort mutates in place (fine here, since we return it). Follow-up: stable sorting with ties — the problem guarantees distinct scores.
